tagline: Thirty miles of marine highway link winding roads on two islands.
intro: The San Juan Islands Scenic Byway joins 30 miles of ferry routes to 85 miles of winding roads on San Juan and Orcas islands. Washington designated it a State Scenic Byway in April 2009. The San Juan Islands Visitors Bureau presents the route as a journey through natural beauty, history, arts and culture. Lopez lies on the marine route but outside the official byway. State of Washington Tourism describes a trip to beaches, lighthouses and harbor towns, with a ferry crossing of the Salish Sea between mainland and islands.

An earlier island road linked the American and British military camps during their joint occupation of San Juan Island. The boundary dispute ended in 1872 when German Kaiser Wilhelm I’s arbitration placed the border in Haro Strait. The camps later became the core of the national historical park established in 1966.

Start at Anacortes and take the ferry to San Juan Island, arriving at Friday Harbor. American Camp occupies the southern peninsula; Lime Kiln Point lies on the western shore and Roche Harbor on the northwest coast. A further ferry ride leads to Orcas Village. Continue to Eastsound and nearby Moran State Park, where Mount Constitution’s observation tower overlooks the surrounding waters.

moments.title: San Juan Island National Historical Park
moments.text: At American Camp, two officers’ quarters and the laundress’s house and working quarters survive from the military occupation of San Juan Island. The confrontation began in 1859 after an American killed a British-owned pig. American settlers requested military protection, Britain sent naval ships, and the two sides agreed to maintain camps while diplomacy settled the boundary. The park encompasses both American Camp in the south and English Camp in the northwest. At English Camp, the Lummi Nation is working to renew traditional uses, including reef net fishing. Congress created the park in 1966.

moments.title: Lime Kiln Point State Park
moments.text: A restored lime kiln and a working lighthouse share this stretch of San Juan Island’s western shore. Kilns operated here beginning in 1860; the first light came in 1914, using acetylene. Five years later, a 38-foot octagonal concrete tower rose from the fog-signal building. The Coast Guard automated the light in 1962. The beacon guides ships through Haro Straits, while the park’s interpretive center explains orcas and the former lime industry. The tower’s first fourth-order Fresnel lens was lit on June 30, 1919; photoelectric cells later switched the automated light on at dusk.

moments.title: Roche Harbor
moments.text: Preserved lime kilns mark Roche Harbor’s earlier life as an industrial waterfront. Limestone came down from higher ground by rail, dropped through chutes into the kilns, then left as processed lime bagged or barreled near the wharf. The company’s ships carried lime along the West Coast, including to San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake. In 1956, the Tarte family bought Roche Harbor and developed the town into a boating resort. The hotel, general store and cottages remain in active use. The harbor faces Haro Strait and the Canada–United States border.

moments.title: Moran State Park
moments.text: Mount Constitution’s stone observation tower grew out of eight years of Civilian Conservation Corps work at Moran State Park. Twenty-eight men from the 4768th Company began building it in August 1935 to a design by Seattle architect Ellsworth Storey. The park began with land donated in 1921 by shipbuilder Robert Moran, whose Orcas Island estate included the Rosario mansion. The mansion and its grounds remain privately owned. The tower stands atop the islands’ highest point, 2,407-foot Mount Constitution, with views across the water. Below the summit, the park includes forests, wetlands, bogs, hills and lakes.
